lead: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through a transmission medium. It sounds simple, and it is, once you can name its parts. Every chat message, UPI payment and IRCTC booking follows the same five-part pattern: a message, a sender, a receiver, a medium and a protocol. Naming the parts tells you where a failure sits and which layer is expected to fix it. This chapter defines those five components, lists how data is represented, then sorts traffic by direction of flow and by type of connection.

blocks.text: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices through a transmission medium. The two devices must be part of one system: a file copied to a pen drive and carried across the room is not data communication.

Message is the data itself, for example the text of a UPI payment note. Sender is the device that sends it, your phone. Receiver is the device that gets it, the bank's server. Medium is the physical path, the Wi-Fi link and the optical fibre behind it. Protocol is the agreed set of rules, HTTPS running over TCP/IP. Remove any one and nothing arrives: with no medium the message has nowhere to travel, and with no protocol it is a signal the receiver cannot interpret. Protocols get a full treatment in 1.4.

The sender is a computer. Inside the sender and receiver the chain splits further: a transmitter (a modem or network card) puts the bits on the medium as a signal and a receiver turns the signal back into bits. The destination is the computer that uses the bits. The figure shows that chain, with the message and the protocol sitting above it. Which box does which job is decided by the device's layer, covered in 1.8.
Data is anything two programs agree to call data. Five forms cover almost every exam question.

items: Text: characters coded as numbers, in ASCII or Unicode. The word Hi is two code points.
Numbers: stored in binary, not as characters. Integers use binary place values, fractions use floating point.
Images: a grid of pixels, each pixel a colour code such as an RGB triple.
Audio: a continuous pressure wave, sampled at fixed intervals so each sample becomes a number.
Video: a sequence of images plus the time order in which to show them.

blocks.text: One medium can carry all five forms, because each is first converted into a signal. The shape of that signal, and how it weakens over distance, belongs to Unit 2.
Some syllabi call these transmission modes. There are three.

Simplex is one direction only, always. A keyboard sends to a computer, a TV tower sends to your set-top box, and a server streams a bank statement that your app only displays: the statement data itself moves one way, and the app never sends anything back on that stream. No reverse channel exists, so the receiver cannot report an error back. Simplex works only when the protocol is fixed in advance, because the receiver has no way to ask for a repeat.

Half-duplex is both directions, one at a time. A walkie-talkie is the standard example: you press to talk and say over to hand the channel back. The link must turn around between the two directions, and that turnaround costs both time and capacity.

blocks.where: U is the utilisation of a half-duplex link as a fraction; T_data is the time spent carrying useful data, in seconds; T_turn is the lost time while the line reverses direction, in seconds. Multiply U by 100 for a percentage.

blocks.text: Full-duplex is both directions at once. A telephone call, a video call and most fibre links are full-duplex. It needs either two separate paths or a way to keep the two directions apart on one path.

A connection is point-to-point or multipoint. Point-to-point joins exactly two devices: a TV remote and the TV, or a leased line between two offices. Multipoint, also called multi-drop, is one link shared by three or more devices: the coaxial cable of an old Ethernet, or one Wi-Fi channel with twenty laptops on it. Multipoint saves cable and ports, but each device then needs rules for taking its turn; those rules are the multiple access protocols of Unit 3. Span and ownership of the whole network are a separate question, in 1.2, and the pattern of links is the topology of 1.3.

Three criteria judge any network. Performance is how fast and how steadily data moves, measured by transit time and response time. Reliability is how rarely the network fails, how quickly it recovers, and how much damage one failure does. Security is protection of data from unauthorised access, change or destruction.

examples.question: An IRCTC user books a ticket from a phone and the app shows a PNR. (a) Name the five components for this transfer. (b) Give the flow mode for each case: (i) the bank pushes a statement to your app and you can only read it; (ii) a teller terminal sends one request and waits for the reply before sending the next; (iii) two engineers talk on a video call. (c) On the teller link a request takes 200 ms to send and the reply takes 100 ms, and every direction change costs 20 ms of turnaround. Find the total time for one request-reply exchange on a half-duplex line and on a full-duplex line, and the percentage lost to turnaround.
steps: (a) Message = the booking request and the PNR screen. Sender = the phone. Receiver = the IRCTC server. Medium = the mobile data or Wi-Fi link plus the provider's network. Protocol = HTTPS over TCP/IP.
(b)(i) Statement push: simplex, one direction only, no reverse channel.
(b)(ii) Request then reply: half-duplex, both directions but one at a time, with the line turning around between them.
(b)(iii) Video call: full-duplex, both directions at the same time.
(c) Half-duplex needs two turnarounds. Time = 200 ms request + 20 ms turn + 100 ms reply + 20 ms turn = 340 ms.
(c) Full-duplex sends both directions at once, so the turnarounds disappear. Time = 200 ms + 100 ms = 300 ms.
(c) Loss = 340 ms − 300 ms = 40 ms. Percentage lost = 100 × 40 ÷ 340 = 11.8 %. Useful fraction U = 300 ÷ 340 = 0.882.
examples.answer: Half-duplex takes 340 ms and full-duplex takes 300 ms for the same exchange, so half-duplex loses 40 ms, about 11.8 % of its time, to turnaround.

half = req + turn + rep + turn

print(half)
print(full)
print(half - full)
print(round(100 * (half - full) / half, 1))

traps: Mixing up sender with transmitter and receiver with destination. The computer is the sender or receiver; the modem or network card is the transmitter or receiver.
Calling an ordinary telephone call half-duplex. A call is full-duplex; the walkie-talkie is the half-duplex example.
Treating simplex as a link with no receiver or no protocol. Simplex still has a protocol and a receiver; only the reverse channel is missing.
Confusing direction of flow (simplex, half-duplex, full-duplex) with type of connection (point-to-point, multipoint). They are two different classifications of the same link.
Listing four components and dropping the medium or the protocol. Examiners count exactly five.

quiz.q: List the five components of a data communication system.
A keyboard sends characters to a computer and can never receive anything back. Which flow mode is this, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: Simplex. It costs the error channel: the receiver cannot ask for a repeat, so the protocol must be correct before transmission starts.

quiz.q: Why is a telephone call full-duplex while a walkie-talkie is half-duplex?
quiz.a: In a call both parties speak and listen at the same time, so two paths exist at once. On a walkie-talkie only one person transmits at a time and the channel must turn around before the other can reply.

quiz.q: A half-duplex link carries 400 ms of request data and 50 ms of reply per exchange, with 25 ms of turnaround at each direction change. Find the total time and the utilisation of the link.
quiz.a: Time = 400 + 25 + 50 + 25 = 500 ms. Useful data time = 450 ms. U = 450 ÷ 500 = 0.90, that is 90 %.

quiz.q: Twenty computers share one coaxial cable in a classroom. Is the connection point-to-point or multipoint? Give one benefit and one new problem it creates.
quiz.a: Multipoint. Benefit: one cable and few ports instead of twenty separate links, so cable cost falls. Problem: all twenty share one capacity and need an access rule to avoid talking over each other, and one break in the shared cable can drop the whole segment.

quiz.q: A modem fails on a link. Using the five components, say which part has failed and why the computer alone cannot fix it.
quiz.a: The transmitter (and the matching receiver at the far end) has failed. The computer still holds the message and the protocol, but without the transmitter the bits never become a signal, so the medium carries nothing.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research radios now try in-band full duplex: sending and receiving on the same frequency at the same time, which classical designs avoided because a transmitter drowns its own receiver. The trick is self-interference cancellation, subtracting a copy of your own signal before it reaches your receiver. Mobile networks in time division duplex (TDD) bands use one frequency and take turns, sending downlink and uplink in different time slots, so the link works like a half-duplex line. Uplink and downlink speeds differ because the frame gives each direction a different share of slots. Frequency division duplex (FDD) uses two separate frequencies and can run both directions at once. Search for in-band full duplex, self-interference cancellation and TDD versus FDD to go further.
